journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Creative Coaching Methods in Career Transition: Exploring Reflection and Meaning-Making Through LEGO ® Serious Play ® and Collage
abstract: This study explores how creative coaching methods may help support reflection and insight in the context of career transition. Eight participants engaged in a facilitated workshop using LEGO ® Serious Play ® and collage to explore experiences of career change and uncertainty. These methods enabled engagement with physical and visual materials to support reflection and meaning-making. Data was collected through pre- and post-workshop questionnaires, photographs of creative artefacts, reflective memos and researcher field notes. Findings suggest that creative methods may enable a nuanced exploration of identity, priorities and future directions and support meaning-making and re-interpretation of perspectives pertaining to career options.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Relational Leadership: An Experience of Relational Methods
abstract: This article provides an account of using relational methods to make sense of the lived experiences of healthcare leaders through narrative interviews, visual artefacts and reflexive approaches. By foregrounding relational identity and reflexivity, this article contributes to leadership and coaching development by offering insight into how leaders, coaches and mentors can cultivate relational awareness within an ethical frame, moving ‘collaborative engagement’ from being a ‘role’ to part of our ‘identity’, values and behaviours.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Integrated Life/Career Coaching for Prelicensure Baccalaureate Nursing Students: An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study of Performance, Well-Being, and Coaching Relationship Outcomes
abstract: The transition from student to practice-ready professional nurse is challenging, particularly for students from disadvantaged backgrounds. This exploratory mixed-methods study reports outcomes of a novel 6-month integrated life/career coaching program for prelicensure baccalaureate nursing students, designed to strengthen essential skills, support well-being, and ease professional transition. Completers reported improvements in academic performance, work performance, and well-being over time. Group differences across coaching effectiveness dimensions did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons, so these results are hypothesis-generating. Integrated coaching models show promise for supporting students with diverse learning and personal needs and enhancing readiness for practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching, Values Alignment and Professional Identity in Contemporary Social Work
abstract: Social work is a values-driven profession practised within increasingly pressurised systems that can obscure practitioners’ original motivations. This study explores whether social workers undertaking coach training perceive greater alignment with their foundational professional values. Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, data was generated from focus groups, semi-structured interviews and collaborative collaging with consultant social workers in adult mental health services in England. Findings suggest coaching reawakens professional identity, strengthens values alignment and enhances reflective capacity, while systemic pressures continue to constrain enactment. Implications for practice education, supervision and workforce sustainability are discussed.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Revisiting the Functions of Coaching Supervision: From Capability to Capacity in Support of CPPD
abstract: In today's context of increasing complexity and uncertainty, coaching is shifting from a predominantly performance and goal-oriented practice towards one that works at deeper levels of identity, meaning and purpose. Alongside this, coaches are increasingly supporting clients experiencing mental health challenges and greater emotional complexity. This shift is accelerated by the growth of AI coaching platforms, which can meet many routine coaching needs. While the demands of coaching are changing, coaching supervision has not developed at the same pace and remains focused on developing competence and capability. There is limited empirical research and conceptual thinking underpinning coaching supervision. In this paper, we critically examine existing supervision functions and approaches and argue that coaches require supervision that fosters the reflexivity and capacity needed to work effectively in conditions of uncertainty and complexity. We propose a conceptual framework to support this shift, equipping coaches to work at these deeper levels of practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: The Impact of Managerial Coaching on Generation Z Employee Retention in Information Technology Startups: The Mediating Role of Affective Commitment and the Moderating Effect of Employer Branding
abstract: This study investigates the impact of managerial coaching on the retention of Generation Z employees in Iranian information technology startups, addressing the research gap concerning the combined influence of coaching, affective commitment, and employer branding. Affective commitment is examined as a mediating mechanism, while employer branding is tested as a moderating factor. Employing a descriptive–correlational design with an applied orientation, the findings demonstrate that managerial coaching significantly enhances retention, both directly and indirectly through affective commitment, with employer branding strengthening these relationships. The results provide meaningful implications for sustainable human resource management practices.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Developmental Mentoring and Career Readiness Among Undergraduate Students in Nigeria: The Sequential Mediating Roles of Career Adaptability and Career Self-Efficacy
abstract: Graduate unemployment remains persistent across sub-Saharan Africa, making career readiness central to higher-education policy. This study examines associations between developmental mentoring and career readiness among 385 Nigerian undergraduates with mentoring experience, and the roles of career adaptability and career self-efficacy. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling showed that developmental mentoring was positively associated with career adaptability (β = .56), career self-efficacy (β = .39) and career readiness through significant individual and serial indirect paths. These findings are consistent with Career Construction Theory and Social Cognitive Career Theory. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis identified two configurations associated with high career readiness, including one where high self-efficacy compensated for lower adaptability. However, the cross-sectional, single-source design precludes causal inference. The findings suggest that structured university mentoring designed to strengthen adaptability and self-efficacy may support career readiness, while differentiated provision could reflect students’ resources.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: An Exploration of Group Coaching for Leaders in Transition to Senior Leadership Positions
abstract: The move into senior leadership has been identified as one of the hardest and can be uniquely challenging for leaders. This two-phase study examined the current challenges leaders face in transition and led to the development of a group coaching programme that was applied and explored through two cycles of action research. The findings evidenced how group coaching can both support leaders through transition in the workplace and develop collective leadership capacity. Theoretical contributions include identifying how group coaching worked to support leaders, and practical contributions include a two-part framework for coaches to use to implement group coaching.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching Collaboratively for a Greater Good with the Planet as a Stakeholder
abstract: The growing urgency of the climate crisis raises questions about the role of coaching beyond individual development, yet empirical research remains limited. This study explored how eco-engaged coaches embed climate responsibility into their role. Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, 13 coaches were interviewed. Findings suggest climate responsibility is embedded within a holistic worldview characterised by interconnectedness, ecocentrism and global citizenship. This is reflected in a values-led, emergent, integrative and relational way of being that extends coaching beyond the individual while maintaining client autonomy. An emergent model suggests that for these coaches, coaching is understood as a collaborative process for social good, with the planet as a stakeholder.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: An Exploration of Coaches’ Perceptions Regarding the Emergence of Artificial Intelligence in Coaching
abstract: This study explores how professional coaches perceive and navigate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into their practice. Twelve professionally trained coaches, with between 3- and 22-years’ experience and working across seven countries, were interviewed, and the data were analysed using Constructivist Grounded Theory and Situational Analysis. The study generates a substantive, exploratory theory of paradigm negotiation: an active, recursive process of boundary-setting, value clarification, and identity reconfiguration through which the participating coaches made sense of AI. Rather than adopting binary pro- or anti-AI positions, participants distinguished between operational augmentation and ethical substitution and articulated what is here termed the absent self as the boundary they drew between human and artificial coaching. Across the accounts, AI operated as a stress test that, for these participants, exposed the limits of behaviourally focused competency models. As a small qualitative study, its findings are offered for analytic transferability rather than statistical generalisation.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching Boundary Development as Values–Identity Realignment: A Constructivist Grounded Theory Study
abstract: Coaching literature often frames boundary struggles as skill deficits, yet highly conscientious professionals frequently fail to sustain boundaries despite adequate technique. Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, this study analysed 12 interviews conducted 1–10 years after a boundary coaching programme. Three theoretical contributions emerged: Stage Zero, a pre-self-authorship developmental position; the Values–Boundaries Paradox, in which cherished values inhibit self-protection; and Permission, an embodied mechanism enabling values–identity realignment. Findings reframe boundary coaching as developmental identity work rather than skills training, with implications for coaching assessment, intervention design and sustainable change.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Development and Initial Validation of the Research Mentoring Context Scale for Undergraduate Research: A Hierarchical Two-Dimensional Measurement Model
abstract: Undergraduate research mentoring is a vital factor in how students engage with their scholarly work. This area presents a gap, as it has not been measured thoroughly, especially in developing higher education contexts. To address this, the present study set out to develop and conduct an initial validation of the Research Mentoring Context Scale (RMCS), drawing on the tenets of both Relational Mentoring Theory and Social Cognitive Theory. Using a cross-sectional instrument development design, data from 453 undergraduates were analyzed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. The results showed a hierarchical two-factor structure that captures positive and negative mentoring environments, with acceptable evidence of reliability, content, and structural validity. The RMCS provides a theoretically grounded tool for assessing mentoring conditions and informing institutional strategies to strengthen undergraduate research development and supervision practices.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Book Review: Mental Health in Coaching Practice: Approaches to Navigate Intersecting Spaces by Calleja, Anne, and Clidière, Ursula CallejaAnneClidièreUrsula. (2027). Mental Health in Coaching Practice: Approaches to Navigate Intersecting Spaces. Routledge, PaperbackISBN: 9781032942971, HardbackISBN: 9781032942988, eBookISBN: 9781003570004

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Beyond Symptom Management: The Socratic Intention Method for Stress Dissolution in Coaching
abstract: Chronic stress has reached epidemic levels in Western societies, with a majority of adults in Germany reporting frequent or occasional stress. Yet many widely used interventions mainly treat the downstream symptoms of stress rather than its cognitive roots. This conceptual paper presents the Socratic Intention Method (SIM), a practitioner-developed framework for stress dissolution that builds on the transactional model of stress and on Stress Inoculation Training. The SIM proposes that chronic stress is maintained not only by unhelpful appraisal but by the psychological usefulness that stress-sustaining beliefs provide, a mechanism consistent with the wider literature on motivated reasoning and belief-based utility. The model introduces three related constructs: (a) stress-sustaining belief functions, six practitioner-derived motivational categories that explain why people hold on to stress-generating convictions; (b) a two-stage dissolution process that combines Socratic questioning with intentional goal-substitution; and (c) the Creator Perspective (Schöpferstandpunkt), a stance related to internal locus of control, self-efficacy, and dispositional optimism, each of which has bee

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Book Review: The Future of Coaching: Building Bridges Between Science and Practice by Greif, Siegfried GreifSiegfried (2025). The Future of Coaching: Building Bridges Between Science and Practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: The Effects of Virtually Simulated Instructional Coaching Practice on In-Service Teachers’ Feelings of Preparedness to Coach
abstract: This study employed a crossover randomized-controlled mixed-methods design to compare the experiences of a diverse group of in-service teachers preparing to be instructional coaches engaged in virtual simulation activities and a standard online module of materials. Quantitative data (n = 22) was analyzed using t-tests and qualitative data using open coding and thematic approaches. Quantitative analyses showed no statistically significant differences in self-reported measures of preparedness to coach or in the helpfulness of the activities. Qualitative analyses showed both conditions were seen as beneficial and identified how the virtual simulation activities could be more impactful on their learning.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: How Coaches Make Sense of Multiplicity Theories
abstract: The phrase ‘multiplicity of self’ refers to the idea that the human mind consists of multiple and distinct identities, sub-personalities or self-states rather than a single, fixed self. Multiplicity is becoming increasingly popular as a theory upon which to base coaching practice. Though there exist many different multiplicity theories, most coaches are familiar with only one or two theories. Multiplicity theories can be quite different in their philosophy and foundations for practice, and clients may respond more readily to some theories than others based on what makes most sense to the individual. In this study, we examined five different multiplicity theories: phenomenological, neurological and philosophical based, to illustrate some of those similarities and differences. We then spoke to 24 practising coaches to understand their coaching philosophies relative to those differences. We close by offering suggestions to those seeking to be more adaptive in their approach to working with multiplicity.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Formal and Informal Mentoring as Pathways to Leadership Competency Development Among Physician Associates in Federally Qualified Health Centers
abstract: This qualitative descriptive study explored how formal and informal mentoring influence leadership competency development among physician associates practising in United States Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs). Data were collected through an anonymous online survey and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: leadership competency development, structural barriers in FQHC leadership development, and relational mentoring and leadership confidence. Findings suggest that mentoring supports leadership confidence, professional identity, and competency growth, while organisational constraints may limit access to structured development. The study contributes to evidence-based mentoring practice by highlighting mentoring as a workforce leadership development strategy in safety-net healthcare settings.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Proprioceptive Sensemaking: A Relational and Developmental Account of Leadership and Coaching in Complex Organisations
abstract: Leadership unfolds in organisational contexts characterised by uncertainty, interdependence and ongoing change. While organisational sensemaking research explains how organisational meaning emerges through interaction, less attention has been given to the developmental capacities through which leaders become aware of their participation in these interpretive processes. Drawing on organisational sensemaking, organisational learning, constructive-developmental theory and David Bohm's concept of the proprioception of thought, this article develops proprioceptive sensemaking as a developmental account of how leaders may become increasingly aware of their participation in the emergence of organisational meaning. This article then presents the Proprioceptive Sensemaking Coaching framework as one practical implication of this account and discusses its contribution to contemporary coaching theory and practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Book Review: Coaching expertise: Six practical steps for every effective coach by McCormick, Iain McCormickIain (2025). Coaching expertise: Six practical steps for every effective coach. Troubador Publishing. ISBN 978-1836281535

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Evolution of College-Student Mentor Perceptions and Practices: Evidence from a School-Based Programme in India
abstract: This study examines how college student mentors in a structured school-based mentoring programme in India understand and refine effective mentoring qualities over time. Using a qualitative longitudinal design, the study draws on baseline open-ended survey responses from the start of the programme and semi-structured interviews with 17 purposively selected college student mentors at the end of implementation. The data is analysed inductively using the Strauss–Corbin coding approach to examine changes in mentors’ perceptions across programme participation. The analysis identifies shifts in how mentors articulate both functional (e.g. guidance, support) and relational (e.g. empathy, adaptability) aspects of mentoring. Preparedness and accountability emerged as salient qualities through sustained engagement. Findings highlight mentoring as a developmental process in which mentors integrate leadership and relational capabilities. The study offers evidence-based insights for programme design, including mentor training and ongoing support within structured programmes.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: A 15-Year Integrative Review of the Influence of Directive Mentoring and Mentors' Unsolicited Advice on Mentoring Outcomes
abstract: Mentoring profoundly shapes professional development, yet the effects of directive behaviours and unsolicited advice remain poorly understood. This integrative literature review examined how overly directive mentoring influences mentoring experiences and how unsolicited advice affects mentoring relationships, drawing on self-determination theory. A systematic search of Web of Science and EBSCO databases (2010–2025) identified 18 empirical studies. Findings revealed that directiveness and unsolicited advice operate as double-edged practices, capable of both supporting and undermining mentee autonomy, competence and relational quality. Theoretically, this review reconceptualises both constructs as measurable behavioural continua and advocates for future quantitative investigation to advance precision in mentoring research and practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching for Higher Education Students: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Higher education is undergoing rapid social changes that demand renewed justification of its roles. Coaching has emerged as a potentially effective tool to enhance students’ academic performance and well-being, yet the evidence base remains fragmented across outcomes, designs, and delivery formats. This systematic literature review synthesised empirical educational coaching interventions targeting higher education students. Following PRISMA procedures, 25 studies were included after full-text screening at Web of Science and Scopus. Across 85 assessed outcome variables, 71 showed statistically significant improvements, with the most consistent gains in life skills, educational attainment, and career/employability related indicators. Most interventions used coaches embedded in the same institution, potentially facilitating contextual fit and communication. Overall, coaching in higher education appears promising for supporting students’ intra- and interpersonal competencies, academic performance, and career readiness; however, heterogeneity in study designs and outcome reporting limits causal inference and calls for more rigorous, theory-driven trials and longitudinal evaluations.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching Praxis: Weaving Philosophical Foundations and Reflective Practices Into the Art of Coaching
abstract: This article conceives Coaching as praxis—philosophy, reflection, and ethics in action. Drawing on Dewey, Merleau-Ponty, and Freire, the article frames coaching as relational, embodied, and context-sensitive. Existential, phenomenological, constructivist, and pragmatic traditions inform a being–thinking–doing model linking ontological presence, reflective inquiry, and ethical action through recursive feedback. Critical, somatic, and creative reflection are delineated, with supervision articulated as a mechanism for sustaining ethical involvement. Implications for coach education include developmental learning, arts-based pedagogy, reflective portfolios, and ethically grounded supervision, supporting the formation of practitioners who are wise, relational, and responsive within complex settings.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching Versus Therapy: A Quantitative, Qualitative and Conceptual Analysis
abstract: Coaching is widely employed in organisations, which has led to a debate about the differences between coaching and therapy. This study used quantitative, qualitative and conceptual analyses to examine this. The qualitative data suggested that coaches have a clear idea of the differences between modalities. Qualitative data indicated that coaching is seen as having six features: performance versus emotional outcomes, future versus past focus, emphasis on action-based experimentation, the work context, higher client functioning and triadic contracting relationships. However, conceptual analysis suggested that client functioning level, the organisation's input into coaching outcomes, triadic stakeholder relationships and confidentiality are the most important distinctions.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Coaching as a Catalyst to Facilitate Spiritual Leadership
abstract: This study explores how a structured coaching intervention can enhance the development of spiritual leadership within organisational contexts. Drawing on Fry's Spiritual Leadership Theory, the research adopts a longitudinal mixed-method design integrating self-assessment instruments, reflective journals and coaching session transcripts. The findings suggest that coaching supported self-reported growth in leaders’ vision, altruistic love and hope/faith, which participants associated with more ethical decision-making, greater authenticity and improved team engagement. Given the small, purposive sample and the reliance on self-report data, these findings are offered as exploratory and analytically, rather than statistically, generalisable. The study contributes an integrative Spiritual Leadership Coaching Framework and a preliminary theorisation of the mechanism through which coaching may facilitate spiritual leadership development, grounded in a South African, Ubuntu-informed context.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Beyond Competence: Rethinking Team Coaching as a Plural Practice
abstract: In this paper the results of a meta-review of 423 peer-reviewed articles on team effectiveness, plus books and book chapters, are reported. The study was conducted in search of evidence to support the idea there exists a single particular approach to coaching teams. From the study emerged a model comprising 11 themes, different aspects of team effectiveness. The model underwent preliminary testing with a group of 50 team leaders. The results of this study provide no support for the idea that there is one best way to help teams become more effective, indeed the rationale for such an approach is challenged conceptually. Implications for future research are discussed, including research and critical analysis at the individual practitioner level.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Researcher Positionality in Mentoring Research: A Critical Inquiry Into the Construction of Research Design
abstract: Critical mentoring emphasizes reflexive methodologies in educational research and mentoring. The programme analysed in this study provides mentoring for children from underprivileged backgrounds. Social science researchers should consider their positionality when conducting research. The author's position of being an active member (mentor and later supervisor) of the programme helped construct the research and develop the mentoring and supervising practices. The research is embedded in participatory observation, and the mixed-method research focuses on protégés and mentors’ perceptions. Essentially, this article overviews the impact of involvement in the analysed programme on the research design and interprets the data by discussing researcher positionality.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Dating Coaching Using Attachment Theory, Mindfulness, and Self-Compassion: A Case Study
abstract: This case study of coaching for a 55-year-old heterosexual woman to find a relationship through online dating describes a coaching psychology approach informed by the social psychology of dating and relationship science, applying attachment theory, mindfulness, and self-compassion, with intrapersonal and interpersonal development. Ethical considerations specific to dating coaching are discussed, including the boundaries between coaching and therapy.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Executive Coaching and Organisational Commitment: The Role of Goal Agendas
abstract: Executive coaching (EC) is increasingly adopted as a strategic HR development practice, yet the differential effects of distinct EC goal agendas types on organisational commitment remain empirically underexplored. This study examines how performance, skills and life goal agendas influence affective, normative and continuance commitment among 101 Tunisian executives using PLS-SEM. Results reveal that performance agendas significantly enhance affective commitment, while life agendas negatively affect normative commitment; skills agendas yield no significant effect. These findings provide the first agenda-specific evidence of differential commitment outcomes and offer HR practitioners evidence-based recommendations for retention-oriented coaching interventions.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Exploring the Concept of Peer Coaching in a Hierarchical Fire Service
abstract: This qualitative study explores firefighters’ experiences of undertaking a formal coaching role within a hierarchical fire service. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with operational firefighters who had completed the organisation's coaching programme, the research examines how coaching is understood and practised within a command-based environment. Findings suggest that coaching occupies a distinctive organisational position: it is formally sanctioned and aligned with organisational values, yet operates outside the operational chain of command. Participants described coaching as a developmental and relational practice shaped by hierarchy, operational accountability and the need to navigate multiple professional identities. The study also questions the adequacy of the term peer coaching within hierarchical settings, where rank and authority continue to influence coaching relationships. The study contributes to a more contextually grounded understanding of peer coaching within hierarchical organisations.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Executive Mentoring for Financial Advisors: A Strategy for Engagement and High Performance in Career Development
abstract: Financial advisors in fintech-enabled, client-centric environments often lead without formal authority while navigating intense targets, regulation, and constant change. This study develops and evaluates an evidence-informed executive mentoring model designed to boost engagement and sustainable high performance. Using a documentary, exploratory approach, and survey insights from practitioners, we identify the mentoring mechanisms most strongly linked to emotional regulation, resilience, communication, client acquisition, and retention. We translate these findings into a practical, phased framework that firms can implement to accelerate capability building and reduce disengagement in modern advisory settings.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Intellectual Bypass in Executive Coaching: When Self-Awareness Fails to Produce Change
abstract: Self-awareness is widely regarded as a central mechanism of change in executive coaching, yet a theoretically under-explained gap persists between insight and transformation in high-performing client populations. This paper introduces the concept of intellectual bypass to account for this gap: the process by which psychological insight is assimilated into an existing identity structure in service of its continuation rather than its transformation. The framework specifies the mechanism of this assimilation – the recruitment of reflective capacity by a high-investment identity structure as an extension of its organising logic – distinguishes intellectual bypass from three adjacent constructs, and derives conditions under which coaching interventions are more or less likely to interrupt it. Practitioner implications are developed, including a framework for recognising intellectual bypass in session and four concrete shifts in coaching orientation. The construct is derivable from adult developmental psychology, psychodynamic theory, and self-determination theory, and generates a tractable empirical research programme for coaching psychology.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Toward Developing an Initial Program Theory for Cognitive Behavioral Coaching in Organizational Contexts: A Realist Study
abstract: This study addresses the critical question of how cognitive behavioral coaching (CBC) works, why, and under what circumstances, an area with limited existing evidence despite CBC's growing use in organizations. Using a realist approach, the authors tested and refined initial program theories through eight stakeholder interviews, following RAMESES standards to ensure methodological rigor. The analysis yielded 11 program theories across cognitive, behavioral, goal progression, and program implementation themes. The findings advance theoretical understanding by identifying CBC mechanisms and their outcomes, both intended and unintended. Practically, the study offers insights for designing more effective, context-sensitive coaching interventions in workplace settings and highlights directions for future research.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Motivation to Move: Methodology for a Randomized Pilot Trial Comparing a Traditional Versus Coaching-Based Physical Activity Prescription Program on Health Indices and Adherence Among Adults
abstract: Prescription To Get Active (RxTGA) is a community-based organization that partners with healthcare providers and the fitness industry to promote physical activity (PA) through tailored prescriptions. Because enrollment declined during the pandemic, an evidence-based supplement that could be delivered remotely as a support was sought. This randomized pilot trial involved examining the impact of adding Motivational Interviewing via Co-Active Coaching to a traditional 12-week RxTGA offering on health indices and PA adherence among adults. As the first study integrating a validated coaching model into an established prescription program, methodological details will be beneficial for health- and fitness-focused professionals and researchers.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Brief Hybrid Solution-Focused and Cognitive Behavioral Coaching Intervention for Stress Management in SME Executives: A Practitioner's Guide
abstract: Executive managers in small-to-medium enterprises represent a high-risk demographic for occupational stress, yet they are underserved by traditional Employee Assistance Programmes due to severe time constraints. This conceptual paper integrates cognitive behavioral coaching, solution-focused brief therapy, and problem-solving coaching methods into a novel, geographically independent, and cost-effective psychoeducational three-session limited stress management intervention. The article details the framework, sessions, the specific intervention architecture, and a step-by-step implementation strategy. By aligning contrasting modalities, this protocol offers organizational psychologists and coaches a replicable, time-efficient tool to target cognitive stress appraisal and promote resilience, bridging the gap between clinical theory and applied practice.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Applying the MASNI (GASCI) Coaching Model in Mentoring Relationships: A Conceptual Framework for Culturally Aligned Practice
abstract: This conceptual paper applies the MASNI (GASCI) coaching model to mentoring in Southeast Asian contexts. We map its five stages—Matlamat, Alternatif, Strategi, Natijah, and Implementasi—onto mentoring processes, compare MASNI with Western frameworks (GROW, CLEAR, OSCAR), and argue that its explicit ethical-reflection step (Natijah) enhances cultural congruence. Using a narrative review and comparative mapping, we derive propositions and practical guidance for program design, mentor development, and evaluation. The paper positions MASNI as a structured, culturally aligned scaffold for mentoring and identifies a research agenda to test outcomes and mechanisms.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Deriving the Proactive Coaching Integration Framework: A Grounded Theory Study of Managerial Coaching Challenges in Hong Kong's Corporate Sector
abstract: This article presents the development of the Proactive Coaching Integration Framework (PCIF), derived from empirical data collected through a grounded theory study on managerial coaching challenges within Hong Kong's corporate sector. The research involved semistructured interviews with 21 management professionals, aiming to identify prevalent coaching challenges and formulate strategies to address them. Key findings highlight organizational, coaching practice, managerial role, and training and development challenges. The PCIF integrates Proactive Leadership Principles (PLPs) and Distributed Leadership Theory (DLT) to offer a practical, data-driven framework that supports managers in navigating coaching complexities and fostering sustainable organizational growth.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Exploring the Contribution of Mentors in Mentoring Programs for Migrants in Norway
abstract: Mentoring promotes integration of migrants, but little is known about the mechanisms of success. We explore the particular contribution and experience of mentors in mentoring for migrants. We conducted 17 semi-structured interviews with program leaders, mentors and mentees in three mentoring programs in two cities in Norway. Organisational factors, the quality of the relationship between mentors and mentees, type of information given and skills taught are important to facilitate labour market integration and social participation. Mentors valued training, space and opportunity to meet with other mentors and reciprocity. Mentoring in teams (one Norwegian and one peer mentor) was particularly effective.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: An Evaluation of a South African Business Chamber Mentorship Program: Perspectives From Mentors and Mentees
abstract: Mentorship programs are found in academia, workplaces, and professional organizations. Mentoring involves the provision of guidance, knowledge, opportunities, and support by an experienced person (the mentor) for an inexperienced person (the mentee). The purpose of this study was to evaluate a mentorship program run by the Nelson Mandela Chamber of Business. The study used an online survey to collect data from mentors and mentees. Mentors were asked to rate their ability to mentor. The findings indicate that the mentees found the program more valuable than the mentors. Psychological support and career support were the main benefits.

journal_name: International Journal of Evidence Based Coaching and Mentoring
title: Aphantasia: A Coaching Case Study
abstract: In 1880, Sir Francis Galton was the first to describe a condition where individuals were unable to create mental images. This condition, aphantasia, has many different definitions including as a total congenital absence of visual imagery. There is debate about whether it is a visual processing impairment only or a cluster of broader cognitive ones. This structured composite case study describes a senior executive with aphantasia who came to coaching wanting to improve her self discipline. It presents the client and coaches reflections on the utility of coaching and contains implications for coaching practice in this unusual area.
